claim: With repeated training and recovery, muscles can become stronger.
evidence_excerpt: muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activities overload muscles and bones, making them stronger. | To give your muscles time to recover, rest one full day between exercising each specific muscle group.
limitations: “Can” is appropriately conditional. No individual outcome, dose, mechanism or recovery interval is prescribed in the narration.

claim: The challenge can increase gradually as capacity improves.
evidence_excerpt: Small, progressive changes in overload help the body adapt to the additional stresses while minimizing the risk of injury.
limitations: Progression depends on individual ability and adaptation; this is not a guarantee of continual linear improvement.

claim: The same difficult repetition is not supposed to stay equally difficult forever.
evidence_excerpt: When you can easily do more repetitions of a certain exercise, gradually increase the weight or resistance. | As your muscle mass increases, you'll likely be able to lift weight more easily and for longer periods of time.
limitations: Read as an informal description of potential adaptation to an unchanged task; not a promise that every exercise inevitably becomes easy.

evidence_excerpt: the physiologic benefits of walking are largely specific to the lower body and the cardiovascular system.
limitations: General movement statement; no claims of equal effects on all muscles or systems.

claim: Aerobic effort makes the heart beat faster and breathing increase.
evidence_excerpt: Aerobic activity causes a person’s heart to beat faster, and they will breathe harder than normal.
limitations: The narration specifies aerobic effort; it does not say every slow step produces a large heart-rate increase.

claim: Regular training can improve fitness and capacity over time, including on a treadmill.
evidence_excerpt: This increase in demand increases the efficiency and capacity of the lungs, heart, circulatory system, and exercising muscles.
limitations: General training adaptation, not a treadmill-specific trial or a claim that standing on a stationary belt improves fitness. No exact timeline or guaranteed result.

claim: Rest and manageable progression belong in training.
evidence_excerpt: it is important to increase the amount of physical activity gradually over a period of weeks to months. | To give your muscles time to recover, rest one full day between exercising each specific muscle group.
limitations: Supports recovery and gradual progression generally. The script does not prescribe a universal schedule.

claim: Pain is not the training target; the fictional coach stops an exercise that causes pain.
evidence_excerpt: If a strength training exercise causes pain, stop the exercise.
limitations: The coach scene is fictional; this record checks the physiological/safety principle only. Pain is not equated with ordinary exertion; no diagnosis or individualized prescription is made.

claim: One exhausting session is not an instant upgrade.
evidence_excerpt: Once a person reaches a certain fitness level, he or she is able to progress to higher levels of physical activity by continued overload and adaptation. | As you continue strength training, you may notice improvement in your strength and physical function over time.
limitations: Editorial shorthand for lasting strength/fitness adaptation requiring a process. It does not deny immediate health or mood benefits from a single activity session, or establish a minimum number of sessions.

claim: Training capacities have ordinary uses: stairs, groceries and maintaining daily function.
evidence_excerpt: It may improve your ability to do everyday activities | Everyday activities include climbing stairs, grocery shopping, or cleaning the house.
limitations: Evidence supports general physical function; it does not guarantee any individual can lift a child or regain a lost ability. CDC functional-limitation comparison specifically concerns middle-aged or older adults.

claim: People can also train at home or walk outdoors.
evidence_excerpt: Brisk walking, running, bicycling, jumping rope, and swimming are all examples. | You can do strength training at home or in the gym. | You can do many exercises with little or no equipment.
limitations: Walking being possible outdoors is ordinary activity context; no claim that outdoor activity is superior or that every exercise suits every person. A gym membership is not necessary.
